newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore says ASEAN-EU should avoid sticky issues.
newsitem.headline: Singapore says ASEAN-EU should avoid sticky issues.

text.p: Singapore's foreign minister said on Monday that ASEAN and the European Union (EU) should avoid issues that divide the two entities, such as East Timor and Burma.

Shanmugam Jayakumar, in a written response to questions from Reuters, said a principle of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) was not to comment on the internal situation, nor interfere in the domestic politics, of other countries.

He was speaking ahead of the 12th ASEAN-European Ministerial Meeting (ASMM) in Singapore on February 13-14. This will be followed by the first Asia-Europe Foreign Ministers Meeting (ASEM) on February 15.
"ASEAN-EU relations are definitely maturing...and we should concentrate our activities on the things that bind us, instead of those which divide us," he said.

"We realise and acknowledge that our two regions have different perceptions on democracy and development...However this has not been a serious obstacle to both sides cooperating on many areas of common interest," Jayakumar said.
On East Timor, a former Portuguese colony Indonesia invaded in 1975 and annexed the following year, Jayakumar said: "The issue should not be allowed to complicate ASEAN-EU relations."
"It is an issue which is between Indonesia and Portugal and should not be introduced in the ASEAN-EU level relationship.
"ASEAN-EU relations have made steady progress over the years...and that it should not be bogged down by differences over a bilateral issue between two countries in the respective groupings."
Portugal has been a critic of Indonesia's human rights record in East Timor. Jakarta argues it has brought much needed economic development to the territory.
ASEAN groups Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.
The ASEAN-EU meeting is between the two blocs while ASEM is an inter-governmental forum of individual ASEAN members with China, South Korea, Japan and the 15-nation EU.

Asked what answer ASEAN was likely to give if EU Ministers raised concerns about human rights in Burma, Jayakumar said: "Isolating Myanmar (Burma) or imposing sanctions will be counter-productive and will not contribute to the process of inducing change in Myanmar."
The EU has been critical of Burma's human rights record and ASEAN's relations with Rangoon's military government.
"ASEAN's approach is to integrate Myanmar with the rest of the Southeast Asian community," Jayakumar said.
ASEAN leaders decided at a meeting in Jakarta last year to admit Burma, Cambodia and Laos to the grouping. However, no specific date has been set.
